strengths: Significance: RSD offers a useful efficiency-quality trade-off: one-step inference takes 0.059 s with 174M parameters and 539 MB on an A100, versus 0.643 s for 15-step ResShift and substantially larger resource requirements for OSEDiff and SUPIR.

Empirical scope: Evaluation covers RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR, ImageNet-Test, and DIV2K, using fidelity, full-reference perceptual, and no-reference quality metrics. RSD consistently improves perceptual metrics over SinSR and often retains better fidelity than T2I-based alternatives.

Experimental analysis includes controlled ResShift-VSD and AddSR comparisons, distillation-only results, timestep and loss ablations, a higher-resolution training experiment, complexity measurements, and extensive qualitative examples.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is generally well organized and supplies pseudocode, optimizer and loss hyperparameters, training cost, checkpoints, dataset sources/licenses, and detailed failure cases.
Limitations and ethics are discussed honestly, including hallucinated details, failures on fine structure, and possible deepfake misuse.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed equivalence between the RSD loss and a joint reverse-trajectory KL in Eqs. (9)/(20) is not established. The derivation substitutes forward-noised generator marginals for marginals of the learned Gaussian reverse chain. For arbitrary data, the exact reverse conditional is generally a mixture rather than the fixed-variance Gaussian in Eq. (15), so these distributions are not equal without additional assumptions. This undermines the central claim that RSD, unlike VSD, provably aligns the joint trajectory distribution.

The theory also assumes that the auxiliary model reaches its population MSE optimum and that matching its denoiser to the teacher implies matching LR-HR distributions. Practical training uses only five auxiliary updates per generator update and a restricted network, but no approximation analysis is provided. Appendix A additionally drops the leading minus sign from Proposition 3.1 when relating RSD to SiD/FGM and IBMD, creating an internal inconsistency.

Evidence for superior perceptual realism and reduced hallucination relies on automatic metrics and selected images; there is no human preference study. No-reference metrics can reward fabricated texture, making this especially important for the paper's central perception-versus-fidelity claims.

The stochastic generator is not evaluated across random seeds, despite instability and noise sensitivity being explicit criticisms of competing methods. Results also lack repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and statistical significance tests.

Originality is limited: the authors describe the objective as a discrete conditional variant of IBMD and show that it closely resembles SiD/FGM, while LPIPS, GAN, and multistep training are established components. The claimed applicability to arbitrary DDPMs is not experimentally demonstrated.

Comparisons with T2I methods are partly confounded by different architectures, training data, and resolutions. In the matched 512x512 LSDIR experiment, OSEDiff remains clearly better on CLIPIQA and MUSIQ, tempering the broad claim of comparable T2I-level perceptual quality.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite substantial implementation detail: no accompanying code artifact is identified, and seeds, run-to-run variability, checkpoint-selection criteria, some architectural details, and exact stochastic evaluation procedures are missing.

The ethics discussion understates risk by arguing that ImageNet training makes misuse unlikely. Hallucination is particularly consequential for the paper's suggested medical, autonomous-driving, and remote-sensing applications, none of which are validated here.

strengths: Significance: One-step ResShift inference is practically useful. RSD reports 0.059 s inference, 174M parameters, and 539 MB peak memory, comparing favorably with the 15-step teacher and substantially larger text-to-image systems. The review covers the complete manuscript and supplement. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/ae3c99ee6ca2454a8e2019a2fbbfa40f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical study spans several synthetic and real-world datasets, multiple fidelity and perceptual metrics, official baseline implementations, complexity measurements, and comparisons with SinSR, OSEDiff, SUPIR, VSD, and AddSR.

The distillation-only comparisons provide some evidence that the proposed training objective improves no-reference perceptual scores over SinSR under a shared ResShift setting; the full model also obtains strong LPIPS results.

Presentation and reproducibility: the paper includes pseudocode, major optimizer and loss hyperparameters, training time, dataset and baseline sources, licenses, extensive qualitative examples, and useful ablations of multistep training and supervised losses.

The authors candidly show failure cases involving hallucinated or unrecoverable details and acknowledge dependence on an imperfect teacher. They also discuss deepfake misuse rather than presenting super-resolution as risk-free.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central joint-KL interpretation is not established. In deriving Eq. (20), the paper asserts that the forward conditional q(x_t|x_hat_0,y_0) equals the reverse-model marginal p(x_t|y_0). These are different objects unless the former is first integrated over generated x_hat_0, and even that forward marginal need not equal the marginal of the Gaussian reverse chain defined in Eqs. (14)-(15). Exact reverse conditionals of a noised non-Gaussian data distribution are generally mixtures, not the fixed-variance Gaussian kernels assumed here. Consequently, the claimed equivalence between Eq. (7) and trajectory-level KL, and the asserted advantage of capturing temporal dependencies over VSD, do not follow.

The weighting induced by the claimed Gaussian KL contains eta_{t-1} in the denominator and is singular at t=1 where eta_0=0. The experiments instead omit these theoretically derived weights, but the implications of this mismatch are not analyzed.

Proposition 3.1 is a value-function identity only when the inner fake model reaches its exact population optimum with sufficient capacity. The implementation uses only five alternating fake-model updates per generator update. No approximation bound, convergence evidence, sensitivity to K, or diagnostic showing that the fake model tracks its optimum is provided.

The premise f_G approximately equal to f* implies generated data approximately equal to real data is assumed rather than proved. Moreover, f* is an imperfect learned teacher rather than the true conditional expectation, so matching it does not establish the claimed data-distribution recovery or generalization to arbitrary DDPMs.

Empirical evidence is insufficient for the broad perceptual-quality claims. Results rely heavily on learned no-reference metrics such as CLIPIQA and MUSIQ, which can reward sharp hallucinations; there is no human preference evaluation despite fidelity and hallucination being central motivations. Distillation-only RSD often trades sizable PSNR/SSIM losses for those scores, while the full model's improvements are partly attributable to LPIPS and GAN supervision rather than the new distillation objective.

Reported results use single point estimates without seeds, uncertainty, or significance tests. Dataset sample counts and baseline stochastic sampling or prompt settings are not reported, and the qualitative selections cannot rule out cherry-picking. The complexity comparison is limited to one 64x64 input on an A100 and does not substantiate deployment on consumer devices.

Originality is limited: Appendix A describes the objective as a discrete form of IBMD and closely related to SiD and FGM. Adapting these ideas to latent ResShift with SR-specific losses is useful engineering, but the claimed new general distribution-matching theory is weakened by both this prior work and the invalid KL derivation. Generalization beyond ResShift is not demonstrated.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite helpful pseudocode: no code or checkpoint release is supplied or committed to, and important details such as random seeds, exact timestep schedule, loss-normalization formula, preprocessing, and full evaluation configuration are deferred to inherited repositories or omitted.

Presentation contains substantial notation and exposition problems, including conflating conditional and marginal distributions, overstating metric improvements as distributional evidence, numerous grammatical errors, and qualitative figures that require extreme zooming. These issues make the already delicate theoretical argument difficult to verify.

Ethics treatment is incomplete. The conclusion that misuse risk is low because training used ImageNet is unsupported, and proposed medical, autonomous-driving, and disaster-response benefits are not validated. The paper also reports an unknown license for DRealSR without resolving whether the intended use is permitted. Overall, the method may be practically promising, but the unsupported central theory and evidential gaps are material enough to prevent acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The core alternating-distillation construction is technically plausible, and Proposition 3.1 gives a useful regression-based tractable form for training an auxiliary fake ResShift model. The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering real and synthetic datasets, full images and 512×512 crops, fidelity and perceptual metrics, several model families, and both distilled and fully supervised variants.

Significance: RSD delivers a practically attractive operating point: one-step inference in 0.059 seconds with 174M parameters and 539 MB reported memory, compared with 15-step ResShift and much larger T2I-based systems. It substantially improves perceptual metrics over SinSR while generally retaining better fidelity than aggressively generative T2I approaches.

Evaluation: The paper includes relevant comparisons with ResShift, SinSR, OSEDiff, SUPIR, AddSR, a newly implemented ResShift-VSD baseline, GAN-based methods, and multistep diffusion systems. Tables 5–6 isolate multistep training and the LPIPS/GAN losses, while Appendix E examines 512×512 training to reduce a potential resolution-confounding concern.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is well organized, supplies pseudocode, optimizer and loss hyperparameters, update ratios, training iterations, hardware and runtime, checkpoint information, metric implementations, dataset sources, and extensive supplementary results. Figures and tables are readable and the qualitative examples help expose fidelity–perception tradeoffs.

Limitations and ethics: The authors honestly show failure cases involving hallucinated or unrecoverable fine detail and acknowledge dependence on the imperfect teacher. They also discuss beneficial applications, misinformation risks, dataset licenses, and LLM usage; these disclosures appropriately strengthen rather than weaken the submission. weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed joint-KL interpretation appears insufficiently justified. Appendix A defines p(x0:T|y0) through Gaussian reverse kernels whose means use the optimal conditional predictor, then asserts q(xt|x_hat0,y0)=p(xt|y0). In general, a reverse Gaussian with a conditional-mean parameterization need not reproduce the forward marginal of an arbitrary generated-data distribution; the true reverse conditional can be a non-Gaussian mixture. Thus Equations 9 and 20 and the claimed joint-trajectory interpretation do not follow without additional assumptions. The regression identity in Proposition 3.1 may remain useful independently, but the paper should separate that valid identity from the stronger KL claim.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. The appendix shows close relationships to SiD, FGM, and especially describes RSD as a discrete conditional-IBMD objective. Much of the practical system combines this related auxiliary-model objective with established ResShift initialization, multistep training, LPIPS, and GAN losses. The precise novelty relative to conditional IBMD should therefore be framed more narrowly.

The strongest final-model gains cannot be attributed solely to the proposed distillation objective. On RealSR, distillation-only RSD improves no-reference scores over SinSR but loses about 1.2 dB PSNR; much of the final LPIPS/fidelity improvement comes from established supervised LPIPS and GAN components. Table 6 is helpful, but comparisons using the same auxiliary losses with alternative distillation objectives would better isolate the contribution.

The evidence relies heavily on automated image-quality metrics, particularly no-reference CLIPIQA and MUSIQ, without a human preference study. These metrics can reward sharp but unfaithful hallucinations—the very failure mode motivating the work—and results are mixed against T2I baselines: OSEDiff or other methods remain better on several MUSIQ, MANIQA, NIQE, DISTS, PSNR, and SSIM settings.

Reproducibility is adequate but not complete: the paper gives no multiple-seed variability, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or explicit evaluation-set sample counts, and does not clearly commit to releasing the RSD implementation and trained weights. The alternating fake-model/GAN optimization could be sensitive to initialization and stochastic training, making variance evidence particularly valuable.

The societal-impact discussion understates misuse by suggesting low risk merely because training used ImageNet; super-resolution hallucinations can still alter evidentiary details. DRealSR is also listed with an unknown license. These are manageable concerns, but the deployment warning and data-governance discussion should be more careful.
